During the 1780's, he authored a series of works known as "The Continentalist." Later, he founded the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, which sought to build an ideal industrial town in Paterson, New Jersey. From 1799 to his death, he served as President General of the hereditary Society of Cincinnatus, a post that critics used to accuse him of monarchism. More controversial was his affair with Maria Reynolds and his payment of hush money to her husband, and although unknown at the time, his most boneheaded move might have been the intentional creation of a national debt—even worse than agreing to a July 12, 1804 meeting with Aaron Burr. Name this first Secretary of the Treasury.

He worked with Franz Liszt for a musical setting of his story The Golden Legend. His early works include "The Battle of Lovell's Pond" and Hyperion, while his first collection, Voices of the Night, was criticized by Poe. He followed that up with a drama called The Spanish Student, but achieved much greater success with the 1854 publication of a narrative poem, the rhythms of which he based on the Kalevala. The only American writer buried in Poet's Corner in Westminster Abbey, name this author of "The Courtship of Miles Standish" and "Hiawatha."

This poem's persona calls upon his addressee to "Come to the window, sweet is the night air!" However, his mournful tone is exemplified by the "grating roar/Of pebbles which the waves draw back, and fling... With tremulous cadence slow." This eternal note of sadness, he says, was heard by Sophocles on the Aegean. Closing with the image of the lovers standing on a "darkling plain... Where ignorant armies clash by night," is, what Matthew Arnold poem set at a seaside?

His affair with C.P. Snow's future wife ended when this man married Caitlin Macnamara, whom he called "Betty Boop" in their extensive correspondence. At his death, he left unfinished the autobiographical Adventures in the Skin Trade. His prose includes 1953's film script The Doctor and the Devils and the 1940 story collection, in satire of Joyce, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog. Two of his most popular works were published after his death: the "play for voices" Under Milk Wood and the short story "A Child's Christmas in Wales." name this Welsh poet best known for the 1946 poem "Fern Hill" and the 1951 villanelle "Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night."

In 1896 Ralph Griffith translated it into English, though the first Western language translation of it was an edition combined with Sayana's commentaries on it by Max Mueller. The text has been dated back to the second millennium B.C. Based on references to the Sarasvati River and the Aryan invasion theory, and is divided into ten books called Mandalas. Containing hymns to such deities as Purusha, Indra, and Agni, what is this early Hindu text that precedes the Sama, Yajur, and Atharva in the series of four Vedas?

As a youth, he is first seen alone at boarding school reading about Orson and Valentine from As You Like It, as well as Ali Baba and Robinson Crusoe. A subsequent scene reveals that his father has grown "much kinder than he used to be" and that the girl with him, Fan, would grow up to be the late mother of his nephew Fred. He also revisits the tragic moment when his fiancée Belle dumped him for displacing her with "a golden [idol]" after watching his youthful self and Dick Wilkins prepare for a holiday party hosted by his mentor, Mr. Fezziwig. These scenes all occur when one of four sprits appears to, what former partner of Jacob Marley, who undergoes a change of heart in Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol?

In one scene, the name of a mysterious character named Lemkin is evoked as one character threatens to get his supervisor fired. Another character mentioned only by name is Jerry Graff, a former employee who left to start a rival company with a less antagonistic office culture. The deadbeat couple Bruce and Harriett Nyborg and the henpecked James Lingk are two examples of clients encountered by Dave Moss, George Aaronow, Ricky Roma, and Shelley Levene, all of whom work at Mitch and Murray's and are pitted in a contest with their salesman jobs at stake. Name this drama about a cutthroat real estate business by David Mamet.

The author describes an affinity for ponds in "During the Long Rains in the Fifth Month" and describes a sunrise in the "Ninth Month" in "I Remember a Clear Morning." The author also denotes summer as the season "To Meet One's Lover" and extols the beauty of pear and plum blossoms in "Flowering Trees." Seeing self-confident men, hearing celebrated poetry, acquiring Michinoku paper, and receiving favor from the Empress above the other ladies-in-waiting appear in the list of "Pleasing Things" included in this Heian Period collection. Name this Japanese court diary that Sei Shonagon may have kept beside her bed.

There are several instances of implied cannibalism in this work, such as where people are drugged to be used as ingredients in dumplings. One of the title characters is considered a descendent of the mythical god-hero from Romance of the Three Kingdoms. This detailed novel traces the origins of each character and how they ended up on Mount Liangshang, whose names were immortalized in stone after a lightning strike as 36 Heaven elements and 72 Earth elements. Together they squelched three rebellions of the Sung Dynasty. Name this novel that criticized the rampant corruption and injustice of the Sung government, written by Shi Nai'an and Luo Guanzhong and known in translation by any of a host of fraternal and wetlands-based titles.

As editor of the Literary Review, his son "Bron" created the "Bad Sex Award" for the worst erotic writing of the year. Late in his career, this author returned to his early style to write about Whispering Glades funeral home and Happier Hunting Ground pet cemetery in The Loved One. His overtly religious work includes a story about Constantine's mother, Helena, and an examination of World War II as a struggle with absolute evil, the Men at Arms trilogy. The satirical novels that established his career include Black Mischief, Vile Bodies, Decline and Fall, and Scoop. Identify this English author whose who used his own conversion to Catholicism for the story of the Marchmain family in his more sober novel Brideshead Revisited.

The fourth stanza in this poem emulates Andrew Marvell by contemplating a plentiful nature of time before the toast and tea. Starting out on half- deserted streets, the poem winds through what appears to be a salon gathering, and ends with visions of a drowning in the sea, surrounded by mermaids and interrupted by human voices. Unsure of himself, the title character wonders whether he should have been "a pair of ragged claws/Scuttling across the silent seas." name this poem about an insecure man who is either an attendant lord, or at times, the Fool, who hears the women "come and go, talking of Michelangelo" according to T.S. Eliot.
The Lovesong of J. Alfred Prufrock

In one section of this work, the main character is about to be killed by a robber but is saved by a robber girl who insists that the main character be kept as her playmate. Eventually, the robber girl sets the main character free on a reindeer, who takes her to Lapland, where she is warmed by the Lapland woman. In Finland, the Reindeer asks the Finland woman for a potion to give the main character the strength of twelve men in order to defeat the title character, but the Finland woman replies that it would do no good. Beginning with the story of a mischievous sprite, this work recounts how a mirror that would reflect and amplify emotions was shattered and pierced the heart of a boy whose grandmother had told him the story of the leader of the white bees. Centering around Gerda's attempts to rescue Kay, identify this Hans Christian Andersen story whose title character is a cold female ruler.

Felix Voorhies and, in Pouponne et Balthazar, Sidonie de la Houssaye were among the authors who adapted it to local settings. The title character's trip down the Mississippi River is something that did not happen during the event described, but by the end of the nineteenth century, many readers regarded this story as a true historical account. It reunites the central characters during an epidemic in Philadelphia after opening with a description of "Le Grand Dérangement" interrupting the wedding of Miss Bellefontaine. Gabriel Lajeunesse and the title character are first separated during the expulsion of Acadians from Nova Scotia in, what Henry Wadsworth Longfellow epic, one of the few English poems in dactylic hexamater?

The collective noun for a group of polar bears is this term. Canadian Science Fiction and Fantasy works can win prizes with this name. In the Marvel universe, she was a member of Alpha Flight and the sister of North Star. She was the person who pricked her finger on a spinning needle and became a slumbering princess in Disney's Sleeping Beauty. In Roman mythology, she was the daughter of Theia and Hyperion and was the goddess of the dawn. This word also describes the luminous atmospheric phenomenon caused by solar wind when coupled with Australis and Borealis or Polaris.

His shorter works include an essay on Victor Hugo for The Corhnill and the stories "Thrawn Janet" and "The Merry Men." He eventually married Frances Osbourne and moved to Samoa; this tuberculosis sufferer's earlier travels in search of a warm climate inspired works such as Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes and, after a canoe trip through France and Belgium, An Inland Voyage. His earlier works include a history of the Covenanters in The Pentland Rising and The Master of Ballantrae. Identify the Scottish author of Kidnapped, The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, and Treasure Island.

He often used popular culture to mark the turning points in his work; in one, a mother's breaking of a treasured collection of jazz records is viewed as a breaking point for the Bergers, who also talk heavily about the Brooklyn Dodgers. Prior to his premature death, he gave up drama to go to Hollywood, where he wrote the screenplays to Wild in the Country and the story of a newspaperman run amok in The Sweet Smell of Success. Name this playwright of "Awake and Sing!" who told of a striking taxi company and a man who falls into a boxing career in Waiting for Lefty and Golden Boy.

In his later years, he wrote several unsuccessful plays, including The Feeble Sex and The Candidate. A relentless perfectionist, he spent decades refining his Memoirs of a Mad Man, which detailed the passionate chasing of a MILF. The influence of Spinoza and Spencer is seen in his Temptation of Saint Anthony. This author had several bumbling "booksmart" title heroes including Bouvard and Pecuchet, and his defining work was translated into English by Gerard Manley Hopkins. Name this French author of The Sentimental Education who told of Bourlanger and the unhappy Emma in Madame Bovary.

One man ultimately falls for the daughter of a tradesman, earning himself a dowry of ten thousand pounds. Another man leaves for Yorkshire upon learning of his aunt's illness, and, upon returning, he saves Harriet from a band of gypsies. An act of rudeness at the strawberry party in Donwell causes Jane Fairfax and Miss Bates to take offense. Ultimately, the novel ends with marriage for the title character and a move to Hartfield. Name this novel whose characters include Reverend Elton, Robert Martin and George Knightly, a work by Jane Austen.

He escapes from cannibals to Salabat and soon after finds a pepper- farming island on which husbands are buried alive with dead wives. After escaping an elephant who throws a tree at him and seeing his ship destroyed by a thrown stone, the old man of the sea latches on to his back and forces him to run around as that man urinates on him. He meets the King of Cassel and finds the valley of diamonds before encountering a roc and relating his adventures to a namesake porter. Name this man who sets out from Basra on seven voyages in the Arabian Nights.

In his later years he focused on illustrating books such as Stephane Mallarme's Poesies and his own book Jazz, and he also created Stations of the Cross, stained glass windows, and vestments for Venice's Chapel of the Rosary. His Harmony in Red was an odalisque from his Nice period, and a representation of his Woman on a High stool can be found in his The Piano Lesson. Creator of works such as Goldfish and The Joy of Life, identify this French artist and leader of the Fauvist movement.

Its characters include Lu Po, who was involved with the beautiful Tiao Shan, and Ssu-Ma, the patriarch of a powerful family. Kuan Yu antagonizes Sun Ch'uan, and Chu-ko Liang advises conciliation with Wu. The establishment of Liu Pei's alliance with Sun Chu'uan led to a crushing defeat of Ts'ao Ts'ao and establishment of a balance of power among the title entities. Identify this Lo Kuan Chung novel set after the defeat of the Yellow Turban rebellion which provides a narrative account of a Chinese historical period.

This author's protagonists include: a man who goes to jail with Stener after loving Ailen Bulter while married to Lillian Semple; the mistress of Charlie Drouet and George Hurstwood; a lover of Lester Kane who is impregnanted by Senator Brander; and a collar-factory employee who yearns for Sondra Finchley and kills Roberta Alden. Frank Algernon Cowperwood, Clyde Griffiths, Jennie Gerhardt, and Caroline Meeber are characters created by what author of The Financier, Sister Carrie, and An American Tragedy?

This entity has a boogie-woogie rumble that shows up after midnight, and the poet questions why it should be his in "Tell Me." According to "Same in Blues," "there's a certain amount of" traveling, nothing, and impotence in it, but it's better known for what the poet asks if it does. It might "stink like rotten meat," or "crust and sugar over," or "fester like a sore." It might sag "like a heavy load," or "dry up like a raisin in the sun." identify this common motif in "Harlem" and other Langston Hughes poems, which completes his question "What happens to..."

The title character fights a hundred men to save the drunken poet Lignere and foils the plot of a scheming nobleman who plans to have the main female character wedded to Valvert so that he can cheat on Cardinal Richelieu's niece with her. The author based much of this play on a biography written by Le Bret, and in real life the title character did indeed fight at the battle of Arras, where, in the play, Christian de Neuvillette is killed by the first shot. Identify this play based on the life of a seventeenth- century nobleman with a really big nose, by Edmond Rostand.

When cornered, he pleads ignorance of "the delicacies of…German philosophy" and wonders if "a maiden lady on Clapham Common" or an evolving ape is more suited to his profession than he is. A predecessor described by this name died through his faith in a hygienic mixture of chalk and water as a substitute for milk. The detective is elected to a seven member executive board, where all but one of the members are actually other undercover detectives and only the leader is actually an anarchist. Name this persona adopted by Gregory Syme who, in a novel by G.K. Chesterton, answers to the leader known as Sunday.
The Man Who was Thursday: A Nightmare

One of the few not to use apostrophe describes how a lover first kissed the author on the hand, then the forehead, then the lips. Another implores that lover to call the author by "my pet-name", while a third explains that "God's gifts put man's best dreams to shame." Better-known ones say that "love, mere love, is beautiful indeed" and question whether the lover would miss her if she died. Taking their title from that pet-name, identify this collection of 44 poems, the best-known of which starts, "How do I love thee? Let me count the ways," by Elizabeth Barrett Browning.

This work takes place during the festival of Bendis in Piraeus, and begins in the home of Cephalus. One character defines the central concept as a simple restraint on pleonexia, but his opponent eventually reveals that the greatest threat is unchecked eroticism. In Book 2, Glaucon brings up the Ring of Gyges, but the turning point occurs in Book 7 when the central character agrees that elenchus should only be taught to the prepared, handing a partial victory to Thrasymachus, and gives a lecture about the awareness of forms via the allegories of the line, the sun, and the cave. Name this dialogue that introduces the concept of the philosopher king and debates the meaning of justice, by Plato.

One character suggests pining away by the Humber while another is set "by the Indian Ganges side" hunting rubies. The poet claims to see "Deserts of vast eternity," during which no more "in thy marble vault shall sound / My echoing song." Even though its addressee's state might begin "ten years before the Flood" and last "till the conversion of the Jews," the poet proposes "Let us roll all our strength and all / Our sweetness up into one ball" after admonishing of the sense of urgency caused by "time's winged chariot." name this famous seduction poem that begins "Had we but world enough and time..." by Andrew Marvell.

His critical works include a study of the prayer of St. Francis of Asisi, Instrument of Thy Peace. His literary career began after his departure from a Boys' Reformatory in Diepkloof, an episode described in his autobiography Towards the Mountain. With Krishna Shah he produced the play Sponono, a reworking of the collection Tales from a Troubled Land. He is also known for the story of Pieter van Vlaanderen, Too Late the Phalarope. Ah, but Your Land is Beautiful continues themes from his best work, in which Arthur Jarvis is murdered by Absolon Kumalo. Name this author of Cry, the Beloved Country.

The title character of this novel is able to corroborate an award for valor in Montenegro and his membership on the Oxford cricket team, but some suspicion is cast on his other achievements when the scholar Owl Eyes discovers that, as real as his books are, they have never been cracked. His dealings with Meyer Wolfsheim and the loss of his true love, who eventually causes his downfall by killing Myrtle Wilson, eventually come out through the correspondence of Jordan Baker with Nick Carraway. Name this novel about a millionaire who renews his relationship with Daisy Buchanan, by F. Scott Fitzgerald.

It begins with the death of Queen Vashti at the hands of an angry King Xerxes, and ends after the plotting Haman is hung upon the 75 foot gallows he constructs for Mordecai and the triumphant of the Jews. This is all due to the bold intercession of the title woman, who is "lovely in form and features." The action in this book begins as three men walk the road to the Thatched House together. Their discourse involves the relative merits of each man's recreational pleasure, and they appeal to sources such as Aristotle and the Bible for justification. Despite the copious details, it's far more than just a book on "How to fish for, and dress, the Chavender of Chub." John Cotton revised this book featuring Piscator, Venator, and Auceps that Isaak Walton wrote.

The most extensive extant text of this work was found at Ninevah in the library of Ashurbanipal. Much of the story of the titular character's battle with Humbaba is missing from surviving versions. During the course of his adventures, this leader of Uruk rejects the marriage proposal of the goddess of love, slays a bull, finds Utnapishtim, and sees a snake steal the plant that would restore his youth. Name this Babylonian epic, which gets its name from a friend of Enkidu and the beloved of Ishtar.

It opens on Grand Isle, just off of New Orleans, with a green and yellow parrot hung in a cage outside the door that keeps repeating "Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That's all right!" The protagonist moves to her own apartment and befriends Mademoiselle Reisz, who adopts her as a protégé. Edna Pontellier desires freedom not only from her social responsibilities, but also in her emotional and sexual existence, and finally drowns herself by swimming too far. Leora, the wife of the titular character, dies from the plague on St. Hubert when she smokes a cigarette infested with germs. She had accompanied her husband Martin, the discoverer of the X Principle, on a medical research trip far from their previous homes in Wheatsylvania and Winnemac. Serving as an indictment of the commercial American medical industry, FTP, what is this 1924 novel by Sinclair Lewis?

This author briefly attended Indiana University before beginning a career as a reporter. It is a collection of hymns praising the gods, first passed down orally until it was set down in writing as a collection somewhere around 900 BCE. Vishnu has his origin here, but he is of minor importance, and neither Shiva nor Brahma make an appearance. Aaron, the only Moor besides Othello in a Shakespeare play, becomes the lover of the Roman Empress, a defeated queen of the Goths. The title character sacrifices one of the Gothic queen's sons. Then the title character kills Tamora's remaining sons and serves them to her in a pie. FTP, name this bloody Shakespearean tragedy, made into a 1999 movie starring Robert Reece.

Described as a "happy young fellow," his life changes when his mother runs off with another man, and his father Rashid's career as the "Shah of Blah" is threatened when asked a simple question about truth. For 10 points--name this title character, paired with "the Sea of Stories" in a Salman Rushdie work, the Arabic equivalent of "Aaron."

The fictional author of this work was exposed following the publication of the fourth edition in 1920, necessitating a change in subtitle away from "The Story of a Youth". That so-called author, Emil Sinclair, was also the novel's protagonist, scarred by his relation with Franz Kromer and healed by his relation with the title character, first name Max, and his mother, Frau Eva. For 10 points--name this semi-autobiographical novel of Herman Hesse.

The final stanza exhorts the reader to "take up our quarrel with the foe" and to catch the torch passed by failing hands, on fear of the restless sleep of the dead. Those dead are described in the second stanza as having "lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow." For 10 points--name this 1915 John McCrae poem whose first stanza describes a place where "the poppies blow/Between the crosses row by row."

She is the lady of Satis House, and late in life she helps her cousin Matthew Pocket and his son by giving 900 pounds to their benefactor. Earlier, the disappearance of her fiancé, the convict Compeyson, leads to her bitter world view, and her eccentric habit of wearing her wedding dress. For 10 points--name this woman, keeper of young Estella, in Charles Dickens' Great Expectations.

This work indicts not only the elitist condescension displayed by some Southern whites toward blacks during the early years of the civil rights movement, but also the genre of transparent allegories that reflected the social changes. During a bus ride, pseudo-intellectual Julian enjoys his mother's discomfort at seeing a black woman wearing a hat identical to hers, but he is shattered when she is handbag-whipped and suffers a stroke. In the final chapter, "A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe," the narrator recounts how she almost never spoke at American school, and "White Tigers" describes the story of Fa Mu Lan. Brave Orchid attends the To Keung School of Midwifery, but when she moves to California, supernatural spirits are replaced by white Americans as the definition of "ghosts." Exploring the female Chinese immigrant experience through her mother's talk-stories, FTP, what is this book by Maxine Hong Kingston?
The Woman Warrior: Memoirs of a Girlhood Among Ghosts

His first acclaimed poem, "For the Marriage of Faustus and Helen," which appeared in the collection White Buildings, was intended as a response to Eliot's The Waste Land. He created homages to other great American writers with his references to Dickinson and Whitman in his most celebrated work and with the elegiac poem "At Melville's Tomb." FTP, identify this poet who offed himself in 1932 but managed to finish "The Bridge" before doing so.

"Fucked by a dahlia!" Bernard yells in scene seven of this play, having just been ridiculed by learning that Ezra Chater was not killed by Lord Byron in a duel, but rather journeyed to Martinique in 1810, described a dwarf dahlia, and died there from a monkey bite. The play moves between April 1809 and the modern day, and a table onstage accumulates an inventory of objects from both periods. FTP, name this 1993 play by Tom Stoppard.

Set in feudal times, this book tells the story of the title character's frequent love affairs with various women, all of who are drawn to him because of his good looks and talent. Though it lacks a general narrative, this book's mini-sagas convey general themes about love, lust, and filial piety. Name this 11th century Japanese work of literature, written at the height of the Heian Period by Murasaki Shikibu and sometimes considered the world's oldest novel.

She died of septicemia two weeks after giving birth to her daughter. Shortly after her death, her husband published his memoirs of her, as well as her unfinished novel Maria, or the Wrongs of Women. Considered a liberal feminist due to her emphasis on the individual woman and her rights, she rejected the institution of marriage, though she cohabited with Gilbert Imley and William Godwin. FTP, name this woman, mother of Mary Shelley.

-20-10, name the author from clues A. He wrote a translation of Alice in Wonderland into Russian, finding Russian equivalents for Carrol's puns and calling his, "not the first translation, but the best". B. An accomplished lepidopterist and chess player, he identified and named at least one new butterfly and was invited in 1970 to create chess problems for the U.S. Chess team. C. His more famous works include the novels Pale Fire and Lolita.

His association with Laura Riding, an American poet, led him to settle on the island of Majorca in 1929, which he called home until his death. His translation of Khayyam's Rubaiyat was extremely controversial in his day, and his White Goddess claimed that all modern religions are rooted in an ancient goddess cult. FTP, name this poet, more popularly known as a novelist, who wrote historical fiction such as Claudius the God and I, Claudius.

Characters in this novel include the Self-Taught Man, who believes he can learn the entire sum of human knowledge by reading every book in the library in alphabetical order, and Anny, former lover of the central character, who is constantly reading history books in order to escape the present-day life. It centers on the study of the Marquis de Robellon, a mysterious French aristocrat. Robellon becomes the obsession of Roquentin, and Roquentin's study draws him to the town of Bouville, where he suddenly realizes the true nature of objective reality, which brings about the title affliction. FTP name this existential novel by Jean-Paul Sartre.

For a gas, it is defined as the ambient pressure integrated over the change in volume. For a rotational solid, it is product of the systematic moment of inertia and the angular velocity integrated over the change in angular velocity. When performed by gravity it is always positive. What is this physical quantity, simply defined as the energy expended to apply a force over a given distance, with units of Joules?

Characters in this play include a dim-witted constable named Elbow who arrests people for sexual misconduct. Barnadine is a prisoner who is sentenced to death along with one of the main characters, while Pompey is a clown who works for a mistress named Overdone. The plot revolves around the restriction of sexual freedoms in Vienna, and the hypocrisy of Angelo, who has abandoned Mariana, yet sentences Claudio to death for the same crime. FTP, identify this play by Shakespeare in which Claudio is saved by his sister Isabella, who marries the Duke.

"As you wish" is the only phrase the hero says to Buttercup until right before they are separated. This film is told through a frame narration of a loving grandfather reading the novel to his Cubs-loving grandson, who, despite his protestations to the contrary, is in fact interested in the kissing scenes. The novel features farmboy-turned-pirate Westley seeking first to rescue his lady love from a kidnapping, then from her fiancée, the evil prince Humperdink. Name this film based upon "S. Morgenstern's classic tale of True Love and High Adventure."

In this story people constantly watch their walls and listen to "Seashell radios." The "green bullet" provides a means of communication between the main character and his accomplice. "Dover Beach" is read and mechanical hounds chase non-conformers. Here the "Book People" are the only ones who still have knowledge of literature and philosophy. FTP, name this novel that features 17-year old Clarrise McClellan, fire chief Beartty, Mildred, and the protagonist, Guy Montag, written by Ray Bradbury.

-20-10, name the novel. A. The title character sees an angel at Tabitha's bedside in the night, but is told it is just a hallucination due to a high fever that he has. He later claims that it was the Angel of Death and he had interrupted it. B. The theme of armlessness is iterated through an armadillo, the swaddled Baby Jesus, a vandalized statue of the Virgin Mary, and eventually the death of the title character. C. This 1989 John Irving novel centers on development of faith in John Wheelwright through the sacrifices of his best friend, a preternaturally small boy with a nasal voice, who accidently killed his mother with a foul ball in Little League.

This play revolves around the visit of Jim O'Connor, a former classmate of a girl he remembers as "Blue Roses". During the course of the disastrous evening, he breaks the horn off of her unicorn figurine and reveals that he is already engaged to somebody else. FTP, narrator Tom Wingfield abandons his mother Amanda and crippled sister Laura in what play by Tennessee Williams?

Her second book depicted the life of nine-year old Almanzo, who works on a family farm in upstate New York during the years after the Civil War. Unlike most of this author's other works, Farmer Boy did not concern her childhood, but rather that of her husband. As a girl, this author's family moved from Wisconsin and Minnesota out to the Dakota Territory, as chronicled in such books as On the Banks of Plum Creek and The Long Winter. FTP, who was this author of the "Little House" series?

Set in 1665, this pseudo-historical work depicts events through the eyes of an observer named ‘H.F.' Partly intended as a criticism of the medical practices in England at the time, it features a scene with a bellman walking the streets of London crying "Bring out your dead!" name this novel in which the city is ravaged by Yersinia pestis, written by Daniel Defoe.
A Journal of the Plague Year

It tells of a man and a woman from different social classes, Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza, who fall in love but are kept apart by fate. Instead, Fermina marries a European-educated doctor who falls in love with her during a medical visit, Dr. Juvenal Urbino. The two go through a tumultuous but happy marriage until his death fifty years later. At Juvenal's wake, Florentino approaches Fermina, and after half a century of waiting, he wins her love. FTP, name this novel by Gabriel Garcia Marquez.

His book immediately enters into a story about a creature with wheels, wings, and many faces – the cherubim. After he sees this vision, he is given a scroll to eat, which tasted like honey in his mouth. His early oracles pronounce God's judgement on a sinful nation and the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadrezzar. FTP, name of this major prophet, whose visions are often paralleled in the book of Revelation.

Some of his prose works include The Friend, Lay Sermons, Essays on his Own Times, Aids for Reflection, and Biographia Literaria.
